taxonomic_note: POWO accepts Acer grandidentatum as a distinct species. Historic sugar-maple infraspecific combinations are synonyms/taxonomy references, not proof of eastern Acer saccharum.
look_here_first: Check opposite SIMPLE palmate leaves, then compare sinus depth and leaf undersides: broad 3–5 lobes with relatively shallow notches are typical; short hairs may occur below. Confirm with paired samaras, buds and bark when available. Do not identify from fall color or canyon habitat alone.

project_inclusion.learner_admission_basis: Approved Master Plant Pool row 10; 2026-10-07 taxonomy and diagnostic review; scientific-review-allium-acer-2026-10-07.md
project_inclusion.range_basis: Texas state-native under POWO/source-pool review, but a three-project-target-county native audit is not complete. Do not count in confirmed-native metrics.

morphology_keys.habit: Deciduous maple, often in rocky/canyon woodland; growth site supports but cannot prove ID.
morphology_keys.leaves: Opposite, simple, palmately 3–5-lobed blades; lobes comparatively broad and sinuses often shallower than silver maple; abaxial pubescence varies.
morphology_keys.flowers: Small flowers; use twig/bud and paired winged fruits as secondary corroboration.
morphology_keys.fruits: Paired winged samaras; young fruits can be hairy. Angle alone is not a decisive species character.
best_field_traits: broader lobes and generally shallower sinuses than silver maple
underside can bear short hairs; avoid absolute hair/no-hair rules

comparisons.key_distinctions: Acer saccharinum has usually much deeper angular/V-shaped leaf sinuses and a conspicuously pale/silvery underside (some hairs possible). Acer negundo has opposite COMPOUND leaves with 3–5 leaflets. Acer palmatum is an introduced/cultivated ornamental with different leaf dissection; never infer wild local origin.
